notes:
I've drafted notes for Matthew 4, but they're uneven. The temptation section (vv. 1–11) is well covered. Verses 12–16 have some material, and I found nothing specific on verses 13, 24 and 25. I didn't reach any pages from bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org, catholic.com, oca.org, or any prosperity or word-of-faith teacher, so for "other views" there is only one Church Father (Origen, via newadvent.org). Several useful pages also cut off before the end (Enduring Word after v. 9, Gill's full chapter). A second round of searching should target those gaps.

---

## 1–11: The temptation

**v. 1**
- Guzik (Enduring Word) says that just as Jesus identified with sinners at His baptism, Jesus then identified with them again in severe temptation. He adds that Jesus did not need to be tempted to help Him grow. Instead, He endured temptation both so that He could identify with us (Hebrews 2:18 and 4:15), and to demonstrate His own holy, sinless character. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-4/
- Guzik also says the Spirit never tempts anyone, but may lead us to a place where temptation comes. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-4/
- On the word itself, he notes that many commentators believe that isn't accurate, because the word translated tempted here is better understood as tested. https://enduringword.com/blog-archive/weekly-devotionals/tested-by-the-devil/
- A footnote on CCEL makes the same point: the Greek word can also mean "tested." https://www.ccel.org/study/Matthew_4:18-23
- Calvin gives two reasons for the wilderness. One was so that, after the fast, Jesus might come forth as a new man, or rather a heavenly man, to the discharge of his office. The other was that he might be tried by temptation and undergo an apprenticeship before taking up His office. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/calvin/calcom31.ix.xxxi.html
- Gill says Jesus was tempted so He would be like His brothers in every way, and could help the tempted with a man's heart as well as God's power. He also notes the pattern that sharp temptations often follow close fellowship with God. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/matthew-4.html
- Spurgeon: No sooner anointed than assailed. He did not seek temptation, but was "led of the Spirit." https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-4-commentary-spurgeon
- Matthew Henry: The assurance of our sonship is the best preparative for temptation. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mat/Mat_004.cfm
- Contending for the Faith (StudyLight) contrasts Adam, who fell in a beautiful garden, with the second Adam, who won in a wilderness. It cites Lenski's view that Jesus was tested "to the finish" with Satan's full power. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ctf/matthew-4.html

**v. 2**
- Guzik says the forty days recall Noah and Israel's wilderness years, and that Jesus will succeed where Israel as a nation failed. He calls the fast a time of "forced dependence" on the Father, not self-denial for its own sake. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-4/
- Bible Hub's study notes link the forty days with Moses on Sinai, Elijah's journey to Horeb and Israel's forty years. Where Israel repeatedly failed to trust God amid hunger and testing, Jesus remained obedient. https://biblehub.com/matthew/4-2.htm
- **Debate: was He hungry during the forty days?**
  - Matthew Henry says Jesus was never hungry during the fast, and only afterwards, to show that he was really and truly Man. https://www.ccel.org/h/henry/mhc2/MHC40004.HTM
  - Contending for the Faith reports that McGarvey and Alford think His appetite was miraculously suspended. Lenski thought He forgot His hunger because the temptation absorbed Him. The author himself reads the verse simply as setting up the first temptation. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ctf/matthew-4.html

**v. 3**
- Guzik: "If" is better read as "since." Satan did not doubt Jesus' deity; he dared Him to prove it. He calls it a temptation to use God's gifts for selfish purposes. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-4/
- Gill thinks Satan had been tempting Jesus secretly for the whole forty days, and now appeared openly. He keeps both readings of "if" open: doubting His Sonship, or arguing from it. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/4-3.html
- Spurgeon: Temptations to unbelieving self-help are common enough, but very dangerous. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-4-commentary-spurgeon
- Calvin rejects the old scheme of gluttony, ambition and covetousness as ingenious trifles. A hungry man wanting food is not gluttony. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/calvin/calcom31.ix.xxxi.html
- Matthew Henry says Satan hinted that the Father had abandoned Jesus, much as he told Eve that God was holding back something good. https://www.ccel.org/h/henry/mhc2/MHC40004.HTM
- Contending for the Faith: Adam and Eve were tempted with food and fell; Jesus was tempted with bread and stood firm. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ctf/matthew-4.html

**v. 4**
- Gill gives an unusual reading. The verse does not mainly mean that the soul lives on God's word. It means God is not tied to bread and can sustain life by other means, such as the manna mentioned in Deuteronomy 8:3. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/matthew-4.html
- Kretzmann (Lutheran) quotes Luther: there are two kinds of bread. The first and best bread, which comes down from heaven, is the Word of God; the other and more unimportant is the earthly bread. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kpc/matthew-4.html
- Ellicott: all three of Jesus' answers come from two chapters of Deuteronomy, a part of Scripture every Israelite learned. https://biblehub.com/matthew/4-4.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary adds that the Shema passages of Deuteronomy were the first Scripture taught to a Jewish child. https://biblehub.com/matthew/4-4.htm
- Guzik: Jesus fought as fully man, and He drew on no "special resources" unavailable to us. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-4/
- Matthew Henry: Jesus is Himself the eternal Word and could have spoken fresh revelation. Instead He honoured Scripture and set us an example. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mat/Mat_004.cfm

**vv. 5–6**
- Guzik: the pinnacle stood about 200 feet above the Kidron Valley. Satan wanted Jesus to "force" the Father into a public spectacle. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-4/
- Spurgeon: This second temptation is a cunning one: he is persuaded rather to believe too much than too little. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-4-commentary-spurgeon
- Gill: Satan first tempted Jesus to distrust God's care and now to presume on it. He uses the same trick when people argue from predestination that they need not use ordinary means. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/matthew-4.html
- **Debate: did Satan misquote Psalm 91?**
  - Guzik, quoting Spurgeon and Poole, says Satan left out "to keep you in all your ways" and so twisted the promise. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-4/
  - J. A. Alexander (quoted on Precept Austin) calls the omission theory a gratuitous refinement, as our Lord himself makes no such charge. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-4-commentary
  - Gill, on the Luke parallel, says it is not a clear case to me, what Satan did leave out, or whether any thing at all. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/luke-4.html

**v. 7**
- Matthew Henry: expecting God to rescue us when we deliberately walk into danger, without using the means He has given, this is presumption, this is tempting God. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mat/Mat_004.cfm
- Precept Austin: We tempt God when we "force" Him (or dare Him) to act contrary to His Word. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-4-commentary
- Guzik: do not demand something spectacular from God to prove His love; He already proved it at the cross. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-4/

**vv. 8–9**
- Guzik: the offer was a shortcut around the cross. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-4/
- **Debate: does Satan really control the world's kingdoms?**
  - Guzik says yes. The temptation would not be real unless Satan in some sense possesses the kingdoms. Adam handed this authority over, though God remains the final owner. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-4/
  - Gill calls the offer monstrous arrogance, from a creature who controls nothing at all in the universe. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/matthew-4.html
- **How did Satan show Him the kingdoms?**
  - Guzik quotes Adam Clarke: if taken literally, it must have been a vision. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-4/
  - Kretzmann says the location, and whether it was physical or a mental picture, does not matter. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kpc/matthew-4.html
- Matthew Henry: Satan shows the world's glory and hides the sin, sorrow and death behind it. https://www.ccel.org/h/henry/mhc2/MHC40004.HTM
- Contending for the Faith: after offering a shortcut to popularity, Satan now offers a shortcut to kingship. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ctf/matthew-4.html

**v. 10**
- Gill: the word "only" is not in Deuteronomy. Jesus added it, rightly, because it fits the context. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/matthew-4.html
- Ellicott notes that Peter later heard the same rebuke, "Get thee behind me, Satan," when he tried to turn Jesus away from suffering (Matthew 16:23). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/4-10.htm
- Another commentary collected on Bible Hub says this is the first time Jesus names Satan. Earlier, evil had come in disguise; now it showed its open hostility to God's will. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/4-10.htm
- Spurgeon: No son of God can worship the devil. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-4-commentary-spurgeon
- Contending for the Faith: Deuteronomy 6 first warned Israel in times of plenty, but Jesus quoted it while suffering. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ctf/matthew-4.html

**v. 11**
- Gill: the angels came only after Satan left, that it might appear that Christ alone had got the victory over him. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/matthew-4.html
- Spurgeon: Satan left only for a season, minding to return at the first opportunity. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-4-commentary-spurgeon
- Kretzmann quotes Luther's comfort that many angels serve us while only one devil tempts us. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kpc/matthew-4.html
- Guzik: Jesus gladly ate what the angels brought. The issue was never refusing help from heaven, but waiting for the Father's timing. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-4/

## 12–25: Ministry in Galilee

**v. 12**
- Gill: Herod imprisoned John (see Matthew 14:3). According to Josephus the prison was the fortress of Machaerus. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/matthew-4.html

**v. 14**
- Gill cites a Jewish tradition that the Messiah would be revealed first "in the land of Galilee." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/matthew-4.html

**vv. 15–16**
- Spurgeon: some people are in deeper darkness than others, and there is hope of light for them, all of it found in Christ. He notes that Galilee was known for its heresies, But what a mercy it is that God can save heretics. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe/matthew-4.html
- A commentary on Bible Hub says the people "sat" in darkness by choice, and that the gospel makes day there. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/4-17.htm

**v. 17**
- Guzik: Jesus waited until John was in prison, so He probably saw Himself as picking up where John left off. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-4/
- Bible Hub's study notes: "is near" means God's rule has come close. It is present in Christ but still awaits its full arrival. https://biblehub.com/matthew/4-17.htm
- Wesley's Notes (as labelled on StudyLight) observe that Jesus had preached before. From this point He preached publicly and regularly. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/4-17.html
- Another commentary on Bible Hub (which I couldn't identify) argues the words are the same as John's but the meaning differs. For John, repentance meant amendment; for Jesus it meant a change from within. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/4-17.htm
- MacArthur (gty.org): God had a kingdom, Jesus said, and if you want to be a part you've got to repent and be converted. https://www.gty.org/sermons/2195/fishing-for-men
- Matthew Henry (on StudyLight) holds that the kingdom was not fully come until the Spirit was poured out after the ascension. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/4-17.html

**vv. 18–20**
- Guzik: God usually calls people while they are busy. Quoting Spurgeon, our Lord does not call idlers but fishers. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-4/
- Burgon (Bible Hub): our Lord went first to the fishing-boats and not to the schools. https://biblehub.com/context/matthew/4-17.htm
- Bob Utley (bible.org): in the Old Testament, fishing was often a picture of judgment. Here it is a metaphor of salvation. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21295
- Spurgeon: the disciples followed in order to listen and learn, and then to go and teach what He had taught them. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe/matthew-4.html
- MacArthur: "I will make you" is Jesus' promise to train them. https://www.gty.org/sermons/2195/fishing-for-men
- David Dickson (on StudyLight): choosing such humble men shows how free God's grace is. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/4-17.html

**vv. 21–22**
- Guzik: the four men answered at once, leaving their nets and their father without hesitation. That is what true discipleship looks like. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-4/
- Dickson: Jesus called them in pairs of brothers, which shows that ministry needs cooperation and affection. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/4-17.html

**v. 23**
- Guzik stresses that Jesus was first a preacher and teacher who also healed, not mainly a miracle-worker. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-4/
- Bible Hub notes that the Greek word for "heal" (*therapeuō*) points to the restoring power of His ministry. https://biblehub.com/matthew/4.htm

## Where Protestant teachers differ

- **How Jesus resisted (v. 1, v. 4).**
  - Calvin (Reformed) held that the Spirit so equipped Christ that Satan's darts could not wound Him, meaning it was impossible for sin to touch Him. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/calvin/calcom31.ix.xxxi.html
  - Guzik (Calvary Chapel, close to Pentecostal) stresses that Jesus fought as a man, with no resources we lack. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-4/
  - These are different emphases, not necessarily contradictions.
- **Fasting and Lent (v. 2).**
  - Matthew Henry (English Nonconformist) calls the Catholic link between Lent and this fast a piece of foppery and superstition. https://www.ccel.org/h/henry/mhc2/MHC40004.HTM
  - Luther, quoted by Kretzmann (Lutheran), says Matthew records that the Spirit drove Jesus into the fast so that no one would copy it by their own choice and make a self-willed fast of it. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kpc/matthew-4.html
  - Bible Hub's general notes, by contrast, recommend fasting as a tool for believers. https://biblehub.com/matthew/4.htm
- **Spirit and Scripture (v. 4).** Gill (Baptist) uses this verse against those who, under a pretence of the Spirit, deny the scriptures to be the only rule of faith and practice. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/4-4.htm

## Other views

- **Church Fathers.** Origen (newadvent.org) reads the name Capernaum as a "place of consolation." Preaching began there and, according to three Gospels, so did Jesus' first miracles. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/101510.htm
- **The Lenten link.** One Bible Hub article says the forty days mirror the early church's forty-day preparation for Easter, citing the *Apostolic Constitutions*. https://biblehub.com/q/Why_did_Jesus_fast_40_days.htm
